<div class="fs-sub">The graph is given; you either <strong>move it</strong> (shift, stretch, reflect) or <strong>read a value off it</strong> and feed it in. Two ideas cover everything: <em>outside as it says, inside the opposite</em>, and <em>let w = f(x)</em>. Learn the boxed rules by heart.</div>

## Transformations of y = f(x)

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### Outside vs inside

**Outside** the bracket changes $y$ and does what it says; **inside** changes $x$ and does the opposite.

$$f(x)+a:\ \text{up }a \qquad f(x)-a:\ \text{down }a$$
$$f(x+a):\ \text{left }a \qquad f(x-a):\ \text{right }a$$

[to move a feature, solve "input $=$ old input", e.g. $f(2x-6)$ max where $2x-6=$ old $x$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Stretches

$$a\,f(x):\ \text{vertical stretch}\ \times a \ \ (\text{outside})$$
$$f(ax):\ \text{horizontal stretch}\ \times\tfrac1a \ \ (\text{inside, reciprocal})$$

[$f(2x)$ is **narrower** and $x$-coordinates **halve**; height unchanged]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Reflections

$$-f(x):\ \text{reflect in the } x\text{-axis}$$
$$f(-x):\ \text{reflect in the } y\text{-axis}$$

[reflecting in the $x$-axis swaps a **maximum** and a **minimum**]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### The two modulus graphs

$$\lvert f(x)\rvert:\ \text{flip the below-axis part **up**}$$
$$f(\lvert x\rvert):\ \text{mirror the } x\ge0 \text{ half into } x<0$$

[$f(\lvert x\rvert)$ is always **even** — symmetric about the $y$-axis]{.eg}
:::

::::

## Function of a function

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### The substitution

An expression built out of $f(x)$ — you cannot differentiate it in $x$. Instead:

$$\text{let } w=f(x),\quad \text{read the range of } w \text{ off the graph}$$

It becomes an ordinary function of $w$ on that range.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Max & min on an interval

Once you have $g(w)$ on $a\le w\le b$, the max and min are among:

$$\text{turning points } (g'(w)=0 \text{ in range}) \ \textbf{and}\ \text{both endpoints}$$

[a maximum can hide at an **endpoint**, not a turning point]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Counting solutions

Solve for $w$ first, then count how many $x$ give each $w$.

[a **peak** value has one preimage; a value between $0$ and the peak has two]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Which method? — $x$-count vs value

$$\text{"how many solutions?"}\ \to\ \textbf{Case 1}$$
$$\text{"max / min / range?"}\ \to\ \textbf{Case 2}$$

**Case 1:** solve for $w$, then **count $x$** (draw $y=w$ on $f$, count crossings). **Case 2:** stay in
$w$ — read the range, analyse $g(w)$; never return to $x$.

[$w=1,4$ are values of $f(x)$, **not** the number of solutions]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Where it shows up on Paper 1

**Identify / apply** a transformation; **sketch** an unfamiliar relation; **read** a value off a graph
and use it; **count** roots or intersections. All four are the same two ideas in disguise.
:::

::::

:::::

## Notes

### Outside does as it says; inside does the opposite

Start from $y=f(x)$. A change **outside** the bracket acts on the output $y$, exactly as written:
$f(x)+3$ lifts every point up by $3$. A change **inside** the bracket acts on the input $x$, and it goes
the **opposite** way to what you expect: $f(x+2)$ moves the graph **left**, not right, because the curve
now reaches each height *two earlier*.

The reliable way to place a feature after **any** transformation is to ask *what input to $f$ produces
it*. If $f$ has a maximum at $x=4$, then $f(2x-6)$ has its maximum where the input equals $4$:
$2x-6=4$, so $x=5$.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Base y=f(x) (max at x=1), and three transformations: +2 lifts it, f(x−2) shifts it right, −f(x) reflects it in the x-axis."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(-3,5,400); f=3*np.exp(-(x-1)**2)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6,3.6))
ax.plot(x,f,color='#1f77b4',lw=2,label='y=f(x)')
ax.plot(x,f+2,color='#2ca02c',lw=1.8,ls='--',label='y=f(x)+2  (up 2)')
ax.plot(x,3*np.exp(-(x-3)**2),color='#ff7f0e',lw=1.8,ls='--',label='y=f(x−2)  (right 2)')
ax.plot(x,-f,color='#d62728',lw=1.8,ls='--',label='y=−f(x)  (reflect)')
ax.axhline(0,color='0.6',lw=0.8); ax.axvline(0,color='0.6',lw=0.8)
ax.legend(fontsize=8,loc='upper right'); ax.set_xlabel('x'); ax.set_ylabel('y')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.example}
[Example.]{.lbl} The graph of $y=f(x)$ has a maximum at $(2,5)$. Find the maximum of $y=f(2x)+1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
$+1$ is outside, so the height rises: $5\to6$. $f(2x)$ is inside, so the maximum occurs when the input to
$f$ is $2$: $2x=2\Rightarrow x=1$.

**Answer:** $(1,\,6)$.
:::

::: {.workbox}

:::

### Stretches — and which factor

$a\,f(x)$ multiplies every height by $a$ (a vertical stretch, $x$ unchanged). $f(ax)$ stretches the graph
horizontally by the **reciprocal** $\tfrac1a$: $f(2x)$ is *narrower* and every $x$-coordinate halves, while
heights stay put. The reciprocal is the part everyone forgets.

### The transformation summary — fill it in

Write the **effect** of each transformation yourself, then check.

| Transformation | Effect on the graph |
|---|---|
| $y=f(x)+a$ | |
| $y=f(x+a)$ | |
| $y=a\,f(x)$ | |
| $y=f(ax)$ | |
| $y=-f(x)$ | |
| $y=f(-x)$ | |
| $y=\lvert f(x)\rvert$ | |
| $y=f(\lvert x\rvert)$ | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answers
| Transformation | Effect on the graph |
|---|---|
| $y=f(x)+a$ | translate **up** $a$ |
| $y=f(x+a)$ | translate **left** $a$ (inside, opposite) |
| $y=a\,f(x)$ | vertical stretch, factor $a$ |
| $y=f(ax)$ | horizontal stretch, factor $\tfrac1a$ |
| $y=-f(x)$ | reflect in the $x$-axis (max ↔ min) |
| $y=f(-x)$ | reflect in the $y$-axis |
| $y=\lvert f(x)\rvert$ | flip the part below the $x$-axis up |
| $y=f(\lvert x\rvert)$ | keep $x\ge0$, mirror it into $x<0$ (even) |
:::

### $\lvert f(x)\rvert$ versus $f(\lvert x\rvert)$

These look similar and behave completely differently — a favourite trap. The bars **outside**,
$\lvert f(x)\rvert$, act on the *output*: anything below the axis is reflected **up**. The bars
**inside**, $f(\lvert x\rvert)$, act on the *input*: the right-hand half is copied across to the left,
making the graph **even** (symmetric about the $y$-axis).

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Base f=(x−1)(x−3) dashed. Left: |f(x)| flips the dip up. Right: f(|x|) mirrors the x≥0 part into x<0."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(-3,5,600); f=(x-1)*(x-3)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(2,1,figsize=(5.2,7.2))
ax[0].plot(x,f,'--',color='0.6',lw=1.2,label='f(x)'); ax[0].plot(x,np.abs(f),color='#1f77b4',lw=2,label='|f(x)|')
ax[0].axhline(0,color='0.5',lw=0.8); ax[0].axvline(0,color='0.5',lw=0.8)
ax[0].set_title(r'$y=|f(x)|$ — flip the dip up',fontsize=11); ax[0].legend(fontsize=8); ax[0].set_xlabel('x'); ax[0].set_ylabel('y')
fmod=(np.abs(x)-1)*(np.abs(x)-3)
ax[1].plot(x,f,'--',color='0.6',lw=1.2,label='f(x)'); ax[1].plot(x,fmod,color='#1f77b4',lw=2,label='f(|x|)')
ax[1].axhline(0,color='0.5',lw=0.8); ax[1].axvline(0,color='0.5',lw=0.8)
ax[1].set_title(r'$y=f(|x|)$ — mirror the right half',fontsize=11); ax[1].legend(fontsize=8); ax[1].set_xlabel('x'); ax[1].set_ylabel('y')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

### Function of a function — let w = f(x)

When an expression is **built out of $f(x)$** — like $\bigl(f(x)\bigr)^3-3f(x)$ — you cannot
differentiate it in $x$, because you have no formula for $f$. The move is a substitution:

::: {.keyline}
Let $w=f(x)$. Read the **range** of $w$ off the graph. Now it is an ordinary function of $w$.
:::

Then the maximum and minimum of that function of $w$ are found the usual way — but on a **closed
interval**, so you must check the **turning points *and* the endpoints**.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "g(w)=w³−3w on 0<w≤3: minimum −2 at the turning point w=1, maximum 18 at the endpoint w=3."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
w=np.linspace(0,3,400); g=w**3-3*w
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.0,3.4))
ax.plot(w,g,color='#1f77b4',lw=2)
ax.plot(1,-2,'o',color='#d62728'); ax.annotate('min (1, −2)',(1,-2),(1.05,-4.3),color='#d62728',fontsize=9)
ax.plot(3,18,'o',color='#2ca02c'); ax.annotate('max (3, 18)',(3,18),(1.5,15),color='#2ca02c',fontsize=9)
ax.axhline(0,color='0.6',lw=0.8); ax.set_xlim(0,3.1)
ax.set_xlabel('w'); ax.set_ylabel('g(w)'); ax.set_title(r'$g(w)=w^3-3w$ on $(0,3]$',fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.example}
[Example.]{.lbl} The graph of $y=f(x)$ attains its maximum value $3$ and $f(x)>0$ for all $x$. Find the
difference between the maximum and minimum values of $\bigl(f(x)\bigr)^3-3f(x)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
Let $w=f(x)$. From the graph the maximum value is $3$ and $f>0$, so $w$ ranges over $0<w\le3$. Study
$g(w)=w^3-3w$:
$$g'(w)=3w^2-3=0\Rightarrow w=1\ (\text{in range}),\qquad g(1)=-2\ (\text{min}).$$
Check the endpoints: $g(w)\to0$ as $w\to0^{+}$, and $g(3)=27-9=18$ (the max). So the difference is
$$18-(-2)=20.$$

**Answer:** $20$.
:::

::: {.workbox}

:::

The same three steps handle every one of these: **substitute $w=f(x)$ → read the range of $w$ → find the
max and min of the function of $w$, turning points and endpoints.** The only thing that changes is whether
the function of $w$ is a cubic, a quadratic, or something else.

### Counting solutions

To count how many solutions an equation like $\bigl(f(x)\bigr)^2-5f(x)+4=0$ has, **solve for $w=f(x)$
first**, then ask how many $x$ give each value. On a single symmetric "bump" with maximum $5$: $w=4$ (the
peak) has **one** preimage, while $w=1$ (between $0$ and the peak) has **two** — three solutions in total.

::: {.example}
[Example.]{.lbl} The graph of $y=f(x)$ has range $-1\le f(x)\le3$. Find the maximum and minimum values of
$\bigl(f(x)\bigr)^2+1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
Let $w=f(x)\in[-1,3]$, so $g(w)=w^2+1$. The vertex $w=0$ lies **inside** the range, giving the minimum
$g(0)=1$. The maximum is at the endpoint farthest from $0$, namely $w=3$: $g(3)=10$ (bigger than
$g(-1)=2$).

**Answer:** maximum $10$, minimum $1$.
:::

::: {.workbox}

:::

### Which method? — solving for $x$ (Case 1) vs finding a value (Case 2)

Both start with the substitution $w=f(x)$, but they **end differently** — and mixing them up is the
classic slip. First ask *what the question wants*.

**Case 1 — "how many solutions / roots?"** (it wants a **count of $x$**). Solve for $w$ first; then for
**each** $w$-value, count how many $x$ satisfy $f(x)=w$ by drawing the horizontal line $y=w$ on the graph
of $f$ and counting crossings. The answer is the number of **$x$'s**, *not* the number of $w$'s.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**The trap.** For $\bigl(f(x)\bigr)^2-5f(x)+4=0$ you get $w=1$ or $w=4$ — but that is **two values of
$f(x)$**, not the answer. On a bump with maximum $4$: $f(x)=4$ meets the peak **once**, and $f(x)=1$ meets
it **twice** — so **three** solutions, not two. You must go back to $x$.
:::

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Case 1: solve (f(x))²−5f(x)+4=0 → f(x)=1 or 4. On the bump (max 4), y=4 meets once (the peak), y=1 meets twice → 1+2 = 3 solutions in x."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(-3,3,600); f=4*np.exp(-x**2)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6,3.4))
ax.plot(x,f,color='#1f77b4',lw=2,label='y = f(x)')
ax.axhline(4,color='#d62728',ls='--',lw=1.2,label='f = 4  → 1 solution')
ax.axhline(1,color='#2ca02c',ls='--',lw=1.2,label='f = 1  → 2 solutions')
ax.plot(0,4,'o',color='#d62728')
for xi in (-np.sqrt(np.log(4)),np.sqrt(np.log(4))): ax.plot(xi,1,'o',color='#2ca02c')
ax.set_xlabel('x'); ax.set_ylabel('y'); ax.legend(fontsize=8,loc='lower center'); ax.set_ylim(-0.3,4.7)
ax.set_title('1 + 2 = 3 solutions',fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**Case 2 — "maximum / minimum / range / value?"** (it wants a **value**). You **never go back to $x$**.
Substitute $w=f(x)$, read the **range** of $w$ off the graph, and find the max/min of $g(w)$ on that
interval — turning points **and** endpoints. The answer is a value, so $x$ never appears. (The two
examples just above — $(f(x))^3-3f(x)$ and $(f(x))^2+1$ — are Case 2.)

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**The one-line test.** Wants a **count of $x$** → draw the $y=w$ lines on $f$ and count crossings
(Case 1). Wants a **value** → stay in $w$ and analyse $g(w)$ (Case 2).
:::
